title: Who Guards the Constitution? A Former Cabinet Secretary's View
label: 16 September 2026 · Constitutional safeguards
summary: Lord Case, former Cabinet Secretary and head of the Civil Service, gave evidence to the House of Lords Constitution Committee about whether the people who advise the Prime Minister and the monarch can really protect the UK's unwritten constitution. He described the Cabinet Secretary as a second-tier guardian, argued that trust between the Prime Minister, the monarch and their advisers is essential, warned that relying on unwritten rules and personal goodwill is outdated, and said he now favours a written constitution—though he conceded it would be very hard to achieve in normal times.

speakers.label: Lord Case
speakers.name: Lord Case
speakers.role: Former Cabinet Secretary and Head of the Civil Service, UK Government

chapters.title: The Cabinet Secretary as a second-tier guardian
chapters.takeaway: The Cabinet Secretary helps protect the constitution but is not one of its ultimate guardians.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Case, welcome. We're looking at the UK's constitutional safeguards. Let's start with the Cabinet Secretary. What's the role, and would you call the Cabinet Secretary a constitutional guardian?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Good morning, Chair. Yes, but a second-tier guardian, not a top-tier one. The real top-tier guardians are the monarch, the Prime Minister and maybe one or two others. The Cabinet Secretary, the Prime Minister's principal private secretary and the monarch's private secretary are support acts to their bosses. They don't have much separate legal standing of their own.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The main job is to advise the Prime Minister on constitutional matters. Occasionally you might talk to the monarch, but usually via the monarch's private secretary.

chapters.title: Four Prime Ministers, a pandemic and the 'Senex' letter
chapters.takeaway: Trusted relationships and access to predecessors matter more than any rulebook when the constitution is under strain.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: You served four Prime Ministers in quick succession. What did you learn from navigating that?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Most of the lessons are about how political parties work internally, not the constitution itself. But during my time we had a change of monarch, four Prime Ministers, and a global pandemic that put huge strain on how power is shared with Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: What got us through was trusting relationships with key colleagues and being able to call on my predecessors. I'd studied under Lord Hennessy, so I had some academic grounding in the constitution too.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: One example: when Boris Johnson's ministers were resigning en masse, someone around him floated calling a general election to save his premiership. I had to pull out the Lascelles principles and the 1950 'Senex' letter—old guidance on when a monarch can refuse a request to dissolve Parliament—and explain why that wasn't a good idea.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: So does the Cabinet Secretary need to be strong enough to stand up to a powerful Cabinet Minister who thinks public opinion is on his side?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. You need to be confident about what's fact, what's your judgment and what's opinion, and be willing to explain that to a Prime Minister or a Cabinet Minister.

turns.speaker: Baroness Laing of Elderslie
turns.text: So there's an informal group of experienced people who together act as guardians of the constitution?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I'd say so, but I think it's inadequate. I started out celebrating our unwritten constitution. Over time I've become convinced we should move towards a written, codified constitution. I loathe the phrase 'good chaps'—because historically most of these guardians were literally chaps from the same schools, universities and social class. That's not a justifiable way to run a 21st-century G7 economy.

chapters.title: Trust, confidentiality and the limits of advice
chapters.takeaway: The Cabinet Secretary can advise and even resign, but if the Prime Minister ignores the advice, the ultimate check is weak.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You mentioned trust and confidentiality. The Cabinet Secretary and the private secretaries need to have deeply private, complex discussions. Agreed?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Absolutely essential. Just as the Prime Minister and the monarch have confidential conversations, the people supporting them must have a trusting relationship too. That's one reason rapid turnover of private secretaries and Cabinet Secretaries is a bad idea—it stops those relationships forming when the chips are down.

turns.speaker: Lord Beith
turns.text: Did you have to teach Prime Ministers constitutional principles they didn't know?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes. Despite many of them having been to the finest schools and universities, some bits of their education had been missing.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Does the Cabinet Secretary have weaknesses as a guardian? If you couldn't persuade a Prime Minister they were constitutionally wrong, at what point would you resign?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Yes, there are inherent weaknesses. The Prime Minister hires and fires you. If they don't like your advice, they can dismiss you and get someone else. You could resign in protest, but the power dynamic is stacked in the Prime Minister's favour.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord O'Donnell said if something was illegal, that was helpful—you could just say 'Prime Minister, that's illegal'. But if it's not illegal, just constitutionally difficult, resignation might be the last resort.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That's right. But these days a Cabinet Secretary resigning might not have the impact it once would have. They come and go like London buses. It would depend on personalities and context.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: But if you resigned and made it public—'I'm going because you're making a major constitutional mistake'—wouldn't that have an impact?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would, but it's unreliable. That's why I've become more convinced we need to codify these things. Leaving it to the chance of a Cabinet Secretary resigning and making the right fuss seems a flimsy way to alert the nation to something constitutionally dangerous.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Lord Young distinguished between something in a manifesto, which is hard to block, and something that's constitutionally offensive. I suspect you agree.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I couldn't agree more. If an elected Prime Minister, backed by Cabinet and Parliament, is carrying out a manifesto commitment, unelected people—whether the monarch or officials—ultimately have to get out of the way.

chapters.title: Towards a more codified constitution
chapters.takeaway: Lord Case thinks written rules would be better than relying on conventions and goodwill, but says a full written constitution is unlikely without a major crisis.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: You've said you want a more codified constitution. Do you mean putting some conventions into law, or a full written constitution? I'd worry a written constitution would put judges in charge of final decisions.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: Personally I'm at the more radical end—I'd like a written constitution. But I'm a pragmatist. Written constitutions usually only happen after extreme national crises, and we're not there yet.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In the meantime, we could codify some things. The Cabinet Manual is woefully out of date. I produced an updated draft when I was Cabinet Secretary, three or four Prime Ministers ago. All of them said they'd publish it, but none has. And even when published, it has no legal force.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: One example worth legislating: requiring a Deputy Prime Minister. After Boris Johnson nearly ended up on a ventilator, we put arrangements in place to always have a Deputy PM. The Covid inquiry agreed. But the current Prime Minister hasn't appointed one. That's just left to whim.

chapters.title: The golden triangle and who's in charge
chapters.takeaway: The 'golden triangle' of advisers works by sharing information and avoiding surprises, but it's no substitute for clear rules about who takes over if the Prime Minister is unavailable.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: What role does the Prime Minister's principal private secretary play during constitutional decisions?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: That's the least understood corner of what we call the golden triangle—the Prime Minister, the monarch and their key advisers. In my experience, the Prime Minister's private secretary talks to the monarch's private secretary several times a week. It's about a 'no surprises' approach: making sure both ends of St James's Park know what's going on. The Cabinet Secretary only gets involved when it's a serious constitutional issue.

turns.speaker: Lord Cryer
turns.text: On the Deputy Prime Minister point: historically the Leader of the House of Commons was seen as number two. Now we have a First Secretary of State, Louise Haigh. If something happened to the Prime Minister, we assume she'd take over, but it's not clear. We're a $4 trillion economy, a nuclear power—we shouldn't be making assumptions about who's in charge.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: I completely agree. The title First Secretary of State was invented for Peter Mandelson by Gordon Brown. It implies a deputy role, but it's not certain. We shouldn't be in this position.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: You said unelected people have to get out of the way. What if a government has a narrow majority and a minority of the popular vote? Does that change things?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: The principle stays the same. Unelected people—from the monarch to officials—have significant power and influence, but must recognise they're ultimately secondary to an elected government. If the monarch's reserve powers were ever used, they'd need to be very sure of their ground and take broad advice.

turns.speaker: Lord Bellamy
turns.text: Does that mean the monarchy is a weak constitutional safeguard in extreme circumstances?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: In my view, yes.

chapters.title: Can the golden triangle hold when things break down?
chapters.takeaway: The golden triangle is made of advisers, not principals, and its strength depends on shared facts and precedents—but it's still no substitute for a written settlement.

turns.speaker: Lord Burnett of Maldon
turns.text: We're interested in how the golden triangle operates when the engine is breaking down, not just when things are working well.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: A concrete example: during those last days of Boris Johnson's premiership, when someone suggested calling a general election to save him, I immediately phoned the other members of the golden triangle. We stepped up our communication and stood on alert. The job is to exchange information and make sure we're all working from the same facts and precedents, even if the final judgment is for the Prime Minister and the monarch.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: But the golden triangle members are advisers, not principals. We shouldn't elevate them into some fantasy league.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: You said the monarch is a relatively weak safeguard. Would you strengthen it?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No. Strengthening the role of an unelected head of state in a 21st-century democracy would go against the flow of our history. I don't think the backstop should be in Whitehall either. Gatekeepers like Cabinet Secretaries are important, but ultimately these things need to rest in settled law—which points me towards a written constitution.

turns.speaker: Lord Murphy of Torfaen
turns.text: Isn't there a contradiction? You want a written constitution, which would define the monarch's role, but you say the strength of the current system is that it's unwritten.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It's a wonderful essay question. I was brought up to celebrate the flexibility of our unwritten constitution. But having seen it up close, and thinking about who wields power, in whose interests, and how you get rid of them if they're not acting in the public interest—that's led me to think a written constitution might be the right answer.

chapters.title: Pragmatic steps short of a written constitution
chapters.takeaway: Even without a full written constitution, some unwritten rules could be turned into law—especially around who takes over when the Prime Minister is unavailable.

turns.speaker: Lord Jones of Penybont
turns.text: Wales and Scotland have written constitutions—Acts of the UK Parliament—and they work. But a written constitution isn't around the corner. Short of that, what could strengthen our safeguards?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: We could move some critical things from the precedent book or the Cabinet Manual into legislation. For example, right now Parliament is changing the law so a Roman Catholic or Jewish Prime Minister could be involved in appointing Church of England bishops—that's a huge constitutional change.

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: More seriously, we should clarify the order of precedence: who do you call if X or Y is unavailable? We shouldn't be making assumptions. You wouldn't run a business like that, so why run a country that way?

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: Is the constitution overall vulnerable? In what ways?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: We've seen governments ignore precedent and advice drawn from the 'good faith' theory of the constitution. It feels like a growing trend. Things that used to be pencil lines should become inked lines. Personality and context will always matter—I'm not naive—but we should have more certainty.

turns.speaker: Baroness Hamwee
turns.text: If we aimed for a written constitution, would getting there gum up everything else?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: It would be extremely difficult in normal politics. Written constitutions usually come out of large-scale crisis. I'd be very cautious about trying to jump there through the ordinary run of Parliament—look at how House of Lords reform can gum everything up.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you, Lord Case. Is there anything else you'd like to add?

turns.speaker: Lord Case
turns.text: No, thank you. More power to your elbow.
